sentences.text: Dune's number is minus 0.58: the highest of any clinic. On that number, Dune is the worst performer in the cast.
It comes from 12 patients.
Alder is just behind, at minus 0.65, from 30 patients.
If you had to bet on which clinic is truly the worst, would you still pick Dune?
Many analysts would not. They would pull every estimate toward the average, and pull hardest where there is least to go on.
That is the random-effect model, and this episode is about what it buys and what it costs.
Welcome back to Model in Motion.
Today: fixed or random?
So far, each provider has had a number of its own, and we have assumed nothing about those numbers. That is what fixed means.
The alternative assumes something: that the numbers are draws from one bell curve, with a centre and a spread.
Then each estimate is a compromise between the provider's own data and the centre. The weight on its own data is called its reliability.
For Dune, with a spread of 0.33 borrowed from our crowd, the reliability is 0.20. Dune keeps a fifth of its distance from the centre.
Do that for every clinic. Dune moves to minus 1.33. Alder, with more patients, keeps two fifths, and stops at minus 1.18.
The order has flipped. And Elm, which had no estimate at all, now has one.
Now the crowd of two hundred, fitted both ways. Each line joins a provider's fixed-effect estimate to its random-effect one.
Small providers move most. Under 50 patients, a typical reliability is 0.37. Above 200, it is 0.83.
The estimates draw together. Their spread falls from 0.44 to 0.26.
The true spread is 0.33. Fixed effects scatter wider than the truth; random effects, narrower.
What does the pull buy? Accuracy, on average. We know the truth in this crowd, so we can measure the typical error.
It falls from 0.28 to 0.20. For providers under 50 patients, from 0.40 to 0.25.
Now the costs. First, the pull does not know who truly differs. Our six planted providers sit 0.8 from the centre.
Fixed effects put them at 0.67, on average. Random effects, at 0.46.
And fixed effects flag four of the six; random effects, three.
The second cost is subtler. In this crowd, providers with sicker patients truly perform better. The random-effect model assumes there is no such link, and pulls everyone toward one centre.
So its errors follow the case mix. Their correlation with it is 0.35. For fixed effects, 0.06.
The sickest fifth of providers look 0.10 worse than they are. The healthiest fifth, 0.10 better.
Break the link, so that performance and case mix are unrelated, and that correlation vanishes.
So which? If you are judging individual providers, and performance may be tied to case mix, fixed effects.
If you have many tiny providers, or your question is about providers as a population, random effects.
Either way, the estimates feed the same standardization from Episode 11. The choice changes the numbers that go in, not the arithmetic that follows.
And neither one protects you from a risk factor that nobody recorded.
Let's gather it up.
Random effects pull each estimate toward the centre, by its reliability.
The pull buys accuracy on average, and gives every provider an estimate.
It costs you the outliers, and it bends with the case mix.
Fixed effects have a cost of their own that we have not faced. One intercept per provider is a great many intercepts.
Next time: too many intercepts.
This has been Model in Motion. Thanks for following the story.
